lines: You choose first. I choose second—and I can get better odds, whichever die you pick. Higher number wins.
These dice have unusual numbers. For this puzzle, each face is equally likely, and one roll doesn’t affect the other.
Yellow always rolls three. Orange has four twos and two sixes. Yellow beats four of those six faces: a two-thirds chance.
But blue has four fours and two zeros. It beats yellow with every four—also two-thirds.
Switch to blue? Green has three fives and three ones. Its fives beat every blue face. Even its ones beat blue’s zeros. That adds up to twenty-four winning combinations out of thirty-six.
Then orange has better odds against green: its sixes beat every face, and its twos beat green’s ones. Again, twenty-four out of thirty-six.
The advantages form a circle. Every die has a counter with a two-thirds chance.
You can still win—or lose—any roll. Choosing second gives an informed player the advantage.
There’s no best die in this set. The better choice depends on what it’s up against.
objectives: The viewer makes a mental choice and knows the high-number rule before decoding probabilities. Four inspectable large dice presented as a challenge, no dominant lecture title.
Clarify unusual values and mathematical conditions. Reveal each die’s repeated-face signature through local turns; no fair-physical-dice certification.
Build the simplest proof. Keep a single yellow3 as the reference; unfold orange’s six equally likely faces into a shallow semicircle, highlight the four2s that lose and retain the two6s that win.
Let the viewer reconsider. Blue enters as the response to yellow; its four4s and two0s split visibly. Different opposition changes the answer without a new full table.

Green looks weak with ones, then reveals two disjoint winning routes. Use a half-and-half green split: all18 pairs in the5 branch win; in the1 branch, six pairs against blue0s win and twelve against4s lose. Build24/36 from18+6; blocks sized to multiplicity, not four equally weighted value types.

Orange returns as a plausible surprise with two6s. Twelve pairs for6 beat every green face; twelve pairs for2 against green1 win; twelve2-versus5 pairs lose. Build24/36 as12+12, using the established visual grammar but a purposeful re-fold/re-pairing, not replaying another grid.
Keep orange visible as yellow re-enters; the apparently best counter is itself countered. Start closing accumulated matchup marks.
Pull back to all four physical identities with a closed counter-choice loop. Arrow direction explicitly means more likely to beat; show the original first choice still has a response.
Show one losing possible outcome briefly while the2/3 label remains; label it possible outcome, not random experimental result. Put the informed second-choice decision in context.
Settle on the closed loop, then emphasize one die beside two different opponents. Same object, different matchup: the exact opening promise is answered without an engagement outro.

openingExploration.text: You choose first. I choose second—and I can get better odds, whichever die you pick. Higher number wins.
openingExploration.firstFrame: Four large unusual dice on a continuous tactile playing surface. Higher number wins is a short supporting rule. An opposing choice space is visible before any odds labels.
openingExploration.rationale: A conversational challenge gives the viewer agency and explains who chooses when. Better odds is independently truthful; whichever die refers to this exact visible set. No fictional host hands or guaranteed win.
openingExploration.risk: Four objects need adequate scale, stable identities and enough exposed numbers; first frame alone cannot prove hidden labels. Reveal distributions through the sequence.

openingExploration.text: Choose any of these four dice. Whichever you pick, another has better odds against it.
openingExploration.rationale: Strong concise approved-premise candidate. The chosen variant gives choosing order a clearer conversational role and states the winning rule immediately. No performance prediction or owner wording rejection.

openingExploration.text: Which of these dice is the strongest? None of them beats all the others more often.
openingExploration.rationale: Clear central question, but reveals the closing idea before the viewer has made a choice. Still truthful and usable if later comprehension tests favor it.

openingExploration.text: This three beats that six more often.
openingExploration.rationale: A dramatic shorthand for yellow versus orange, but independently misleading:3neverbeats6 in a realized roll. Rejected; later face qualifiers cannot repair it.

openingExploration.text: These dice have no best choice. The advantages go in a circle.
openingExploration.rationale: Truthful concise statement, but without a rule or participation cue may feel like unexplained jargon. It could work with a sufficiently legible first picture, untested here.

endingExploration.text: There’s no best die in this set. The better choice depends on what it’s up against.
endingExploration.rationale: Resolves the opening choice and states exactly what changes: the opponent, not the die. Limited to this set, no generic moral or forced question.

endingExploration.text: It’s rock-paper-scissors hiding inside random rolls.
endingExploration.rationale: Memorable analogy but a less complete closing explanation; may suggest fixed winners or three objects. A visual resemblance can help without making it the final line.

endingExploration.text: Which die would you choose now?
endingExploration.rationale: Would invite comments but repeats a choice whose mathematical limits were just resolved. We prefer settled understanding without a spoken CTA.

runtimeEstimate.method: Lexical whitespace count; speech at145–165words/min gives speech-only bounds. Add provisional4–8seconds for mental choice and proof recognition. Not measured narration or an imposed duration.
runtimeEstimate.renewal: Update after authorized complete speech/audio and visual comprehension review; no padding or forced compression.

cta: No spoken CTA; final choice-dependence insight is stronger without an engagement request. No pinned comment or release copy prepared.
